system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2150-07-17 19:39:00 to 2150-07-20 14:58:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding presented with generalized weakness and chest pain after missing dialysis and experiencing severe diarrhea. He was found to have life-threatening hyperkalemia, which was treated with emergency dialysis. The chest pain was determined to be non-cardiac, likely musculoskeletal, with imaging showing a possible fracture of the left eighth rib. An inpatient capsule endoscopy was performed due to prior failed outpatient attempts, with results pending at discharge. His hand pain, following a fall, was attributed to soft tissue injury or gout flare. He remained stable throughout the admission, with improvement in electrolytes and symptoms, and was discharged home with follow-up plans for GI evaluation, blood sugar monitoring, and medication management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I fell out of bed this morning. I was sitting on the edge trying to grab my phone and just lost balance. I couldn’t get up and was on the floor for about two hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you hit your head or feel dizzy before the fall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I wasn’t dizzy. I just slipped. But now my left arm and leg are sore, especially when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve checked your head and neck with CT scans, and there’s no fracture or bleeding. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank you. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did X-rays on your left hip, knee, elbow, and wrist. No fractures there either. The pain is likely from soft tissue strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. It hurts more when I try to walk or lift my arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage the pain with your current oxycodone and add acetaminophen every eight hours to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I also had a cough this morning—started out of nowhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid in the lungs, but it’s not new. We think it’s related to your heart condition, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart issues before. My last echo showed my heart pumping better now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart function has improved. But you’re still in atrial fibrillation, so we’re keeping an eye on your rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not on blood thinners because of past bleeding, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re continuing your diltiazem and digoxin to control your heart rate safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now, your potassium level came back high—6.1. That’s because you missed dialysis due to the fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I missed my ride. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, high potassium can affect your heart. We gave you insulin and sugar to bring it down, but it went up again to 7.3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take you for emergency dialysis tomorrow morning to correct it. That should bring your levels back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure not to miss dialysis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You completed dialysis about an hour ago. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. A little tired, but the chest tightness I sometimes get is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your repeat potassium is now 4.1—perfect. Your bicarbonate also improved, so your acidosis is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m out of danger now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the immediate risk is gone. We’ll keep monitoring you. Your lungs are clearer today too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your left leg to check for a blood clot because of the swelling and immobility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the ultrasound showed no DVT. That’s excellent. You’re safe to move around more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look stable. Potassium is still good, and your kidney numbers improved—creatinine is down to 3.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My sugars have been high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your glargine and sliding scale insulin. Your last HbA1c was 10.7, so we recommend discussing tighter control with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, it’s hard to keep it down with all these health issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Just keep doing your best. We’ve also noted your phosphate is low today—2.4.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The renal team advised holding your sevelamer yesterday, but you’ll restart it at home to manage phosphate long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re stable, labs are good, and pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual medications. Take acetaminophen for pain as needed. Be careful with your balance—maybe use a walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful. And I won’t miss dialysis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Follow up with your primary doctor in a week. Call if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you with a home health aide to help for a few days. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding presented after a mechanical fall from bed, which caused him to miss hemodialysis. He reported left arm and leg pain but had no head injury or fracture on imaging. His potassium was elevated at 6.1, rising to 7.3 despite initial medical treatment, necessitating emergency hemodialysis. Post-dialysis, his electrolytes normalized, and his symptoms improved. Evaluation ruled out DVT and acute intracranial or spinal injury. He was managed with pain medication, including a new prescription for acetaminophen, and discharged home with instructions to continue all home medications, monitor for symptoms, and prevent future falls.
